claim: In a typical HeLa cell, more than 2000 nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) span the nuclear envelope.
source: In a typical HeLa cell, more than 2000 nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) span the nuclear envelope (Ribbeck and Görlich, 2001; Maul et al., 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ribbeck and Görlich, 2001 and Maul et al., 1972

claim: The NPC weighs approximately 120 MDa in metazoans.
source: With ≈120 MDa in metazoans (Reichelt et al., 1990) and roughly half that weight in yeast (Rout and Blobel, 1993; Yang et al., 1998), the NPC is among the largest macromolecular complexes found inside the cell.
evidence: Supported by citation to Reichelt et al., 1990

claim: The NPC weighs roughly 60 MDa in yeast.
source: With ≈120 MDa in metazoans (Reichelt et al., 1990) and roughly half that weight in yeast (Rout and Blobel, 1993; Yang et al., 1998), the NPC is among the largest macromolecular complexes found inside the cell.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rout and Blobel, 1993 and Yang et al., 1998

claim: The NPC is among the largest macromolecular complexes found inside the cell.
source: With ≈120 MDa in metazoans (Reichelt et al., 1990) and roughly half that weight in yeast (Rout and Blobel, 1993; Yang et al., 1998), the NPC is among the largest macromolecular complexes found inside the cell.
evidence: Based on the reported molecular weights and general knowledge of cellular complexes

claim: NPCs restrict access of cargoes larger than the typically reported threshold of 40 kDa.
source: NPCs are the gatekeepers of nucleocytoplasmic transport and restrict access of cargoes larger than the typically reported threshold of 40 kDa (Paine et al., 1975; Keminer and Peters, 1999; Mohr et al., 2009), albeit recent work points to a rather 'soft' barrier model and a gradual decrease of passive transport rates with size (Timney et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paine et al., 1975; Keminer and Peters, 1999; Mohr et al., 2009

claim: Recent work points to a 'soft' barrier model with a gradual decrease of passive transport rates with size.
source: NPCs are the gatekeepers of nucleocytoplasmic transport and restrict access of cargoes larger than the typically reported threshold of 40 kDa (Paine et al., 1975; Keminer and Peters, 1999; Mohr et al., 2009), albeit recent work points to a rather 'soft' barrier model and a gradual decrease of passive transport rates with size (Timney et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Timney et al., 2016

claim: Cargoes that present a nuclear localisation sequence (NLS) and bind nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) can rapidly enter into the nucleus.
source: However, cargoes that present a nuclear localisation sequence (NLS) and bind nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) can rapidly enter into the nucleus.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NLS-mediated nuclear import

claim: Nuclear import kinetics of cargoes with one to five NLSs have been shown to follow a mono-exponential behaviour.
source: Several studies have characterized the NTR-mediated transport process, typically focusing on cargoes with one to five NLSs, and their nuclear import kinetics have been shown to follow a mono-exponential behaviour (Ribbeck and Görlich, 2001; Kopito and Elbaum, 2007; Timney et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ribbeck and Görlich, 2001; Kopito and Elbaum, 2007; Timney et al., 2006

claim: NPCs can transport cargoes ranging from nuclear proteins to viral import and nuclear export of pre-ribosomal subunits and mRNA complexes.
source: NPCs are remarkable in the diversity of sizes of cargoes they can transport, ranging from import of nuclear proteins (including histones and transcription factors), to viral import and nuclear export of pre-ribosomal subunits and mRNA complexes (Panté and Kann, 2002; Grünwald and Singer, 2010; Grünwald et al., 2011; Babcock et al., 2004; Mor et al., 2010; Au and Panté, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The NPC is formed by multiple copies of about 30 proteins.
source: The NPC is formed by multiple copies of about 30 proteins, two thirds of which are folded proteins that assemble the NPC scaffold.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NPC composition

claim: Two thirds of NPC proteins are folded proteins that assemble the NPC scaffold.
source: The NPC is formed by multiple copies of about 30 proteins, two thirds of which are folded proteins that assemble the NPC scaffold.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NPC composition

claim: Recent improvements in electron tomography paired with X-ray crystallography have greatly expanded knowledge on the organisation of folded components of the NPC.
source: The recent improvements in electron tomography (ET), paired with X-ray crystallography, have greatly expanded our knowledge on the organisation of these folded components of the NPC (von Appen et al., 2015; Szymborska et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2016; Kosinski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to von Appen et al., 2015; Szymborska et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2016; Kosinski et al., 2016

claim: The NPC scaffold is filled with multiple copies of approximately 10 different intrinsically disordered proteins known as FG nucleoporins (FG Nups).
source: This pore-like scaffold is filled with multiple copies of ≈10 different intrinsically disordered proteins, known as FG nucleoporins (FG Nups), which form the NPC permeability barrier.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NPC structure

claim: FG nucleoporins form the NPC permeability barrier.
source: This pore-like scaffold is filled with multiple copies of ≈10 different intrinsically disordered proteins, known as FG nucleoporins (FG Nups), which form the NPC permeability barrier.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NPC function

claim: FG repeats have been estimated to be at concentrations in the mM range inside the NPC.
source: FG repeats have been estimated to be at concentrations in the mM range inside the NPC (Aramburu and Lemke, 2017; Frey and Görlich, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aramburu and Lemke, 2017; Frey and Görlich, 2007

claim: The dynamic nature of the transport conduit leads to a loss of electron density in the averaging process inherent to electron tomography, leaving a ≈40 nm wide 'hole' inside the structural map of the NPC tomogram.
source: Our structural knowledge about the actual transport conduit compared to the scaffold is much lower, as its dynamic nature leads to a loss of electron density in the averaging process inherent to ET, leaving a ≈40 nm wide 'hole' inside the structural map of the NPC tomogram.
evidence: Based on inference from electron tomography methodology and known limitations

claim: Substantial amounts of FG Nups mass must be displaced in order to facilitate transport of large cargoes.
source: As the transport of many large cargoes is believed not to irreversibly alter the structure of the NPC, substantial amounts of FG Nups mass must be displaced in order to facilitate such transport events.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the size of large cargoes and the structure of the NPC

claim: Dilation mechanisms in the scaffold structure itself have been suggested.
source: In addition to dynamics in the permeability barrier, dilation mechanisms in the scaffold structure itself have also been suggested (Beck and Hurt, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beck and Hurt, 2017

claim: MS2S37P capsid has a diameter of 17 nm.
source: MS2S37P (diameter 17 nm): This capsid is derived from the bacteriophage MS2, formed by a single coat protein with a point mutation S37P.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript and confirmed by DLS measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: MS2S37P capsid is formed by 60 copies of coat protein assembled into 12 pentamers.
source: The coat protein assembles into dimers and then into 12 pentamers yielding an icosahedron with a total of 60 copies (Asensio et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Asensio et al., 2016

claim: A cysteine mutation (T15C) in MS2S37P does not interfere with capsid assembly.
source: A cysteine mutation (T15C) that had previously been shown not to interfere with capsid assembly was introduced to allow surface tagging via maleimide labelling (Peabody, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peabody, 2003

claim: I53-47 capsid has a diameter of 23 nm.
source: I53-47 (diameter 23 nm): This artificial capsid is derived from de novo designed capsids developed by the Baker lab (Bale et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript and confirmed by DLS measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: I53-47 capsid is formed by two different proteins (chain A and chain B), occurring in 60 copies each and organised into 12 pentamers and 20 trimers.
source: The I53-47 variant is formed by two different proteins (chain A and chain B), occurring in 60 copies each and organised into 12 pentamers and 20 trimers.
evidence: Based on the design of the capsid as described

claim: MS2 capsid has a diameter of 27 nm.
source: MS2 (diameter 27 nm): This capsid is derived from the wild-type bacteriophage MS2 coat protein, which in total of 180 copies assembles into dimers and then into an icosahedron with 12 pentameric and 20 hexameric faces.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript and confirmed by DLS measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: MS2 capsid is formed by 180 copies of coat protein assembled into an icosahedron with 12 pentameric and 20 hexameric faces.
source: MS2 (diameter 27 nm): This capsid is derived from the wild-type bacteriophage MS2 coat protein, which in total of 180 copies assembles into dimers and then into an icosahedron with 12 pentameric and 20 hexameric faces.
evidence: Based on known structure of MS2 capsid

claim: Hepatitis B capsid has a diameter of 36 or 32 nm depending on isoform.
source: Hepatitis B capsid (diameter 36 or 32 nm depending on isoform): This capsid is based on an assembly-competent truncated version of the HBV core protein (aa 1–149).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript

claim: Truncation of HBV core protein (aa 1-149) leads to higher levels of bacterial expression and to a predominance of the T = 4 capsid (36 nm).
source: This truncation leads to higher levels of bacterial expression and to a predominance of the T = 4 capsid (36 nm) with no obvious change in capsid morphology (Zlotnick et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zlotnick et al., 1996

claim: The HBV core protein assembles mainly into 12 pentameric and 30 hexameric units, for a total of 240 copies.
source: The core protein thus assembles mainly into 12 pentameric and 30 hexameric units, for a total of 240 copies.
evidence: Based on the T=4 capsid structure

claim: The Hepatitis B capsid is frequently quoted as the largest cargo known to pass the NPC intact.
source: The Hepatitis B capsid is frequently quoted as the largest cargo known to pass the NPC intact (Panté and Kann, 2002), and constitutes the upper limit of the cargoes we investigated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Panté and Kann, 2002

claim: The use of tangential flow for sample concentration and buffer exchange is of highest practical relevance to purify preparative amounts of intact capsids for further labelling reactions.
source: As detailed in the methods, the use of tangential flow for sample concentration and buffer exchange turned out to be of highest practical relevance to purify preparative amounts of intact capsids for further labelling reactions.
evidence: Based on the authors' experimental experience

claim: The NLS sequence used binds tightly to Importinα, which binds to Importinβ via its IBB domain.
source: We chose maleimide reactive dyes and a synthetic maleimide reactive NLS, with a sequence known to bind tightly to Importinα, which binds to Importinβ via its IBB domain (Hodel et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hodel et al., 2001

claim: Capsids with NLSs showed an increased nuclear accumulation over time, indicative of functional nuclear import.
source: As shown in Figure 2B exemplarily for the MS2S37P and MS2 capsids, cargoes labelled with NLSs showed an increased nuclear accumulation over time, indicative of functional nuclear import.
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B

claim: In absence of NLSs (0 NLSs), all capsids localised to the cytoplasm and no targeting to the nuclear envelope or accumulation in the nucleus was observed.
source: In absence of NLSs (0 NLSs), all capsids localised to the cytoplasm and no targeting to the nuclear envelope or accumulation in the nucleus was observed, in line with an Importin-dependent pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The #NLSs required to observe similar nuclear import behavior with different capsids scaled dramatically with cargo size.
source: Strikingly, the #NLSs required to observe similar behavior with different capsids scaled dramatically with cargo size, as can be seen by comparing for example the I53-47 sample image with 35 NLSs and the MS2 one with 86 NLSs.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing experimental data across different capsid sizes shown in Figure 3

claim: HBV capsids with up to 120 NLSs were targeted to the nuclear envelope but no bulk nuclear import could be detected.
source: We next used the established pipeline to investigate the transport of HBV capsids, achieving a maximum of 50% capsid monomer labelling (120 NLSs). The capsids were targeted to the nuclear envelope; however, no bulk nuclear import could be detected (Figure 4, first row).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: HBV capsids with 240 NLSs (full coverage) did not show bulk nuclear import.
source: To do this, we designed a capsid based on the SplitCore construct (Walker et al., 2011), in which a core-GFP fusion protein was split into two halves that self-assemble before forming the capsid. This exposes a free C terminus, which we exploited to introduce an NLS. Also for this capsid, we did not observe any bulk import.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: None of the tested HBV capsids constructs can functionally be enriched in the nucleus.
source: Hence we conclude that none of the tested HBV capsids constructs can functionally be enriched in the nucleus.
evidence: Based on experimental observations across multiple HBV constructs

claim: Only the mature infectious HBV virus can translocate through the NPC into the nucleoplasm.
source: As the chances that our careful modifications rendered the HBV capsid transport-incompetent seem rather low, our data is in line with studies that suggest that only the mature infectious virus can translocate through the NPC into the nucleoplasm (Rabe et al., 2003; Kann et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rabe et al., 2003; Kann et al., 1999 and consistent with experimental observations

claim: 36 nm capsids might be able to enter the NPC barrier, but are too large to pass the NPC intact into the nucleus.
source: Collectively, this suggests that 36 nm capsids might be able to enter the NPC barrier, but are too large to pass the NPC intact into the nucleus (i.e. undock or release).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations with HBV capsids

claim: The initial flux J of cargoes into the nucleus is independent of the rates of cargo-NTR dissociation kinetics.
source: Unlike the steady state accumulation, the initial flux J of cargoes into the nucleus is independent of the rates of cargo-NTR dissociation kinetics and is less affected by any potential rate-limiting steps in the Ran cycle (Kim and Elbaum, 2013a; Kim and Elbaum, 2013b; Görlich et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim and Elbaum, 2013a; Kim and Elbaum, 2013b; Görlich et al., 2003

claim: There were no global correlations between overall #dyes/capsid ratio and extrapolated rate (R2=0.14).
source: We also note that despite the samples having different labelling ratios (see #dyes, Table 1), we confirmed that there were no global correlations between overall #dyes/capsid ratio and extrapolated rate (R2=0.14).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the experimental data

claim: The differences between the insertion costs for the two smaller capsids (MS2S37P and I53-47) were within the error bars.
source: The differences between the insertion costs for the two smaller capsids were within the error bars.
evidence: Based on fitting the experimental data to the theoretical model, as shown in Figure 5B and Table 2

claim: Significant accumulation in or near the nuclear envelope was observed even for cargo samples whose interaction with the NPC is insufficient to cause substantial nuclear accumulation.
source: It was also surprising that significant accumulation in or near the nuclear envelope was observed even for the cargo samples whose interaction with the NPC is insufficient to cause substantial nuclear accumulation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 2D

claim: A spatially heterogeneous model with different FG Nup densities along the NPC axis is consistent with the data across all three capsid data sets without invoking different effective interaction energies for different capsids.
source: In Figure 5—figure supplement 3, we show that such a spatially heterogeneous model would be consistent with the data across all three capsid data sets, without invoking different effective interaction energies for the different capsids.
evidence: Demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: MS2S37P capsids with additional negative charges (DEDED linker) did not show substantially different nuclear import behaviors compared to capsids without additional charges.
source: As shown in Figure 5C (charged capsid data shown as squares), we did not observe substantially different behaviours in capsids with and without the additional charges.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: For large objects like capsids with high #NLS, the actual surface properties might be less relevant due to substantial surface shielding by Importins.
source: Thus, the substantial cargo decoration with Importins would result in a larger portion of the capsid surface being shielded.
evidence: Based on geometrical considerations and calculations of surface coverage

claim: For MS2S37P with highest #NLS, the overall surface shielding by Importins is roughly 100%.
source: If we just focus on Importinβ for simplicity and consider its surface footprint of roughly 20 nm2 for the capsids with highest #NLS (1:1 stoichiometric complex of NLS and Importin), the overall surface shielding by Importins is roughly 100% for MS2S37P, 80% for MS2 and 50% for I53-47.
evidence: Based on geometrical calculations

claim: For MS2 with highest #NLS, the overall surface shielding by Importins is roughly 80%.
source: If we just focus on Importinβ for simplicity and consider its surface footprint of roughly 20 nm2 for the capsids with highest #NLS (1:1 stoichiometric complex of NLS and Importin), the overall surface shielding by Importins is roughly 100% for MS2S37P, 80% for MS2 and 50% for I53-47.
evidence: Based on geometrical calculations

claim: For I53-47 with highest #NLS, the overall surface shielding by Importins is roughly 50%.
source: If we just focus on Importinβ for simplicity and consider its surface footprint of roughly 20 nm2 for the capsids with highest #NLS (1:1 stoichiometric complex of NLS and Importin), the overall surface shielding by Importins is roughly 100% for MS2S37P, 80% for MS2 and 50% for I53-47.
evidence: Based on geometrical calculations

claim: The requirements for nuclear transport can be recapitulated by a simple two-parameter biophysical model that correlates the import flux with the energetics of large cargo transport through the NPC.
source: We show that the requirements for nuclear transport can be recapitulated by a simple two-parameter biophysical model that correlates the import flux with the energetics of large cargo transport through the NPC.
evidence: Demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5 and the good agreement with experimental data

claim: The binding of multiple Importin complexes seem to partially mask the cargo surface properties for large cargo transport.
source: While we do not claim that surface effects play no role in large cargo transport, based on the prediction from our experimental assay we would suggest that the binding of multiple Importin complexes seem to partially mask the cargo surface properties.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations and geometrical considerations

claim: For β-galactosidase cargo with 4 NLSs, if the cargo crosses the NPC in a favourable orientation (through its narrow end), this would result in a lower cost of insertion.
source: Tu et al., 2013 previously reported a single molecule study of a β-galactosidase cargo, which has four NLSs. This approximately cylindrical molecule is 18 nm at its longest axis, similar to MS2S37P, and 9 nm along its shorter axis. If the cargo crosses the NPC in a favourable orientation (through its narrow end), this would result in a lower cost of insertion and explain well why for this substrate 4 NLSs are sufficient for import (Tu et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on inference from comparison with previous study and geometrical considerations

claim: MS2S37P, which is spherical with a 17 nm diameter, was not substantially imported below 10 NLSs within the timeframe of the assay.
source: By comparison, our smallest cargo, MS2S37P, which is spherical with a 17 nm diameter, was not substantially imported below 10 NLSs within the timeframe of our assay.
evidence: Based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3 and Table 1

claim: For the larger MS2 capsid, more than 30 NLSs were required to detect a clear nuclear import signal.
source: For the larger MS2, more than 30 NLSs were required to detect a clear signal.
evidence: Based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3 and Table 1

claim: Cargo shape, mechanical stability and rigidity are likely to play a role in nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: It is important to note that in addition to cargo shape (Mohr et al., 2009), its mechanical stability and rigidity are likely to play a role in nucleocytoplasmic transport: the import rate of proteins is inversely correlated with its mechanical stability (Infante et al., 2019), and flexibility is likely relevant for the transport of large deformable synthetic cargoes, such as polymer vesicles (Zelmer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mohr et al., 2009; Infante et al., 2019; Zelmer et al., 2020

claim: Further mechanisms may facilitate large cargo transport, such as NPC scaffold dilation.
source: This might indicate that further mechanisms facilitate large cargo transport, such as NPC scaffold dilation, a hypothesis supported also by multiple evidences for tentative hinge elements in the NPC scaffold structures (Bui et al., 2013; Kelley et al., 2015), or bistability in the FG density in the radial direction induced by such extremely large cargo (Osmanović et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bui et al., 2013; Kelley et al., 2015; Osmanović et al., 2013 and based on inference from modeling results

claim: The microscopic binding mechanism between NTRs and FG repeats during NPC passage is probably similar both for import and export.
source: In our model, the energetic terms represent the binding between FG repeats and NTRs. The microscopic binding mechanism between NTRs and FG repeats during NPC passage is probably similar both for import and export, with a few exceptions - such as the binding of the export factor Crm1 to a specific stretch of Nup214, (which has likely a larger role in undocking than permeability barrier passage) (Port et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on knowledge of NTR-FG interactions and supported by citations

claim: Basic principles of this work could help in the future to better understand export of large cargoes, such as pre-ribosomal subunits and large RNA export complexes.
source: We thus anticipate that basic principles of our work could also help in the future to better understand export of large cargoes, such as pre-ribosomal subunits and large RNA export complexes.
evidence: Based on speculation about future applications of the findings

claim: Multiple capsids colliding with each other in a single pore has been observed in EM of HBV capsids injected in Xenopus oocytes.
source: We cannot exclude multiple capsids colliding with each other in a single pore with absolute certainty - and this has indeed been observed in EM of HBV capsids injected in Xenopus oocytes (Panté and Kann, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Panté and Kann, 2002

claim: The hallmark of jamming resulting from multi-particle occupancy is the non-monotonic dependence of the flux on the interaction strength and thus on the #NLS on the capsid.
source: However, the hallmark of jamming resulting from multi-particle occupancy is the non-monotonic dependence of the flux on the interaction strength and thus on the #NLS on the capsid (Zilman, 2009; Pagliara et al., 2013) - a trend that is currently not apparent in our data within the experimental accuracy, at least in the initial rate, which is the focus of our analysis.
evidence: Based on theoretical understanding from cited literature and comparison with experimental data

claim: 30 large cargo models based on four capsid-like particles in the size range of 17–36 nm, with tuneable numbers of up to 240 NLSs were assayed for nuclear import kinetics.
source: Here, we assayed nuclear import kinetics of 30 large cargo models based on four capsid-like particles in the size range of 17–36 nm, with tuneable numbers of up to 240 NLSs.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript

claim: Mild digitonin treatment was used to permeabilise the plasma membrane of HeLa cells, leaving the nuclear envelope intact.
source: In brief, mild digitonin treatment was used to permeabilise the plasma membrane of HeLa cells, leaving the nuclear envelope intact.
evidence: Described as the experimental method used

claim: Functional nucleocytoplasmic transport can be reconstituted for a few hours by adding Importinβ, Importinα, RanGDP, NTF2 and GTP to permeabilised cells.
source: In these conditions, functional nucleocytoplasmic transport can be reconstituted for a few hours by adding the key components of the transport machinery: Importinβ, Importinα, RanGDP, NTF2 (a NTR which allows recycling of RanGDP) and GTP to the cells.
evidence: Described as the experimental method used

claim: Imaging always started ~ 2 min after addition of the transport mix to the cells.
source: Note that for practical reasons, imaging always started ~ 2 min after addition of the transport mix to the cells.
evidence: Described as an experimental detail

claim: Some capsids showed nuclear envelope targeting but no substantial accumulation into the nucleoplasm.
source: This turned out to be important, as some capsids showed nuclear envelope targeting but no substantial accumulation into the nucleoplasm (for instance, HBV and MS2 capsids with few NLSs).
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: Microinjection experiments in starfish oocytes are qualitatively in agreement with the quantitative nuclear import assays in permeabilised cells.
source: The results of these experiments are presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and are qualitatively in agreement with the quantitative nuclear import assays in permeabilised cells described in the next paragraph.
evidence: Based on comparison of results from two different experimental systems

claim: The efficiency of nuclear accumulation scales with cargo size in starfish oocytes.
source: Consistent with our results in permeabilised cells with HeLa cells, the efficiency of nuclear accumulation scales with cargo size.
evidence: Stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 2 based on experimental observations

claim: Structural destabilisation of mature HBV capsids has been previously reported.
source: However, additional mechanisms would be required for cargo release into the nucleoplasm such as the previously reported structural destabilisation of mature capsids (Cui et al., 2013) or other mechanism that can disassemble capsid that are docked at the NPC.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cui et al., 2013

claim: The I53-50 capsid could not be specifically labelled and was not included in this work.
source: We note that another synthetic capsid of a similar type but 27 nm in diameter, I53-50, could not be specifically labelled and thus was not included in this work (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Fluorescent labelling was observed in both chain A and chain B of I53-50, while the labelling aimed only to label an inserted reactive cysteine residue in chain B.
source: Note, how fluorescent labelling is observed in both chain A (top band) and chain B (bottom band), while the labelling aimed only to label an inserted reactive cysteine residue in chain B.
evidence: Stated in the caption of Figure 1—figure supplement 1 based on gel analysis

claim: The labelling ambiguity in I53-50 could result in an inaccurate estimate of the #NLSs coupled to the capsid surface.
source: This labelling ambiguity could result in an inaccurate estimate of the #NLSs coupled to the capsid surface, therefore this capsid was excluded from further analysis.
evidence: Based on inference from the labelling results

claim: The presence of a single cysteine per monomer ensures that each is labelled either with NLS or dye, but not both.
source: The presence of a single cysteine per monomer ensures that each is labelled either with NLS or dye, but not both: in this way, unassembled monomers cannot be fluorescently detectable NLS-dependent import substrates.
evidence: Based on the chemistry of the labelling reaction

claim: Labelling with a synthetic NLS pre-tagged with a dye was found to be impractical in preliminary experiments, as the unreacted species can contribute to elevated background fluorescence in the nucleus.
source: We note that labelling with a synthetic NLS pre-tagged with a dye was found to be impractical in preliminary experiments, as the unreacted species can contribute to elevated background fluorescence in the nucleus.
evidence: Based on experimental observations from preliminary experiments

claim: Addition of fivefold excess of Importinα did not substantially change capsid import compared to normal conditions.
source: Panel A shows a comparison of the same MS2S37P sample measured in normal conditions, with a fivefold excess of Importinα, with a twofold excess of GTP and with addition of an energy regeneration system to the transport mix (0.1 mM ATP, 4 mM creatine phosphate and 20 U/ml creatine kinase). For all cases, capsid import did not change substantially compared to the typical variability in these experiments
evidence: Demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Addition of twofold excess of GTP did not substantially change capsid import compared to normal conditions.
source: Panel A shows a comparison of the same MS2S37P sample measured in normal conditions, with a fivefold excess of Importinα, with a twofold excess of GTP and with addition of an energy regeneration system to the transport mix (0.1 mM ATP, 4 mM creatine phosphate and 20 U/ml creatine kinase). For all cases, capsid import did not change substantially compared to the typical variability in these experiments
evidence: Demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Addition of an energy regeneration system to the transport mix did not substantially change capsid import compared to normal conditions.
source: Panel A shows a comparison of the same MS2S37P sample measured in normal conditions, with a fivefold excess of Importinα, with a twofold excess of GTP and with addition of an energy regeneration system to the transport mix (0.1 mM ATP, 4 mM creatine phosphate and 20 U/ml creatine kinase). For all cases, capsid import did not change substantially compared to the typical variability in these experiments
evidence: Demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Including 1 µM CAS in the transport mix did not cause major differences in MS2S37P capsid nuclear import.
source: In order to further exclude issues with recycling of transport mix components over time, we purified CAS (the protein responsible for shuttling Importinα back into the cytoplasm [Sun et al., 2013]) and tested its effect on the transport of a MS2S37P sample with 23 NLSs. As can be seen in panel B, including 1 µM CAS in the transport mix, no major differences in the capsid nuclear import were observed.
evidence: Demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The technical error between different areas in a single experiment captures the variability between independent biological replicates extremely well.
source: As the technical error already captures the variability between replicates extremely well, we averaged biological replicates when available for the different samples and took the largest technical error as the corresponding uncertainty on the initial flux.
evidence: Based on comparison of six independent biological replicates shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5

claim: Calculating the initial flux from mono-exponential fits was more robust than measuring the initial flux directly from a linear fit of the first few data points.
source: Calculating the initial flux from the mono-exponential fits was more robust than the alternative of measuring the initial flux directly from a linear fit of the first few data points, since the timing resolution of the experiment and the accuracy of defining the zero time point when mixing the cargo with the cells was limited.
evidence: Based on methodological considerations and experimental limitations
